item.title: Dimagi Naxals? The sages of the Vedas and the Upanishads would qualify today
item.description: Should Narendra Modi or Amit Shah seriously engage with the Vedas in search of validation for their Hindutva project, they may find themselves disappointed.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s newly minted phrase dimagi Naxal – “intellectual Naxal” – is meant to designate an ideological enemy: people whose ideas supposedly endanger the nation by questioning its political direction.

In his Independence Day address this year, Modi warned that although armed Naxalism was nearing its end, its ideological adherents are still a threat. Critics immediately pointed out the phrase’s obvious affinity with the government’s earlier use of the phrase “urban Naxal” to stigmatise academics, activists, intellectuals, and other dissenting voices.

There is, however, an unintended irony in this language. If dimagi Naxal is to mean someone who questions authority, then some of the earliest and most formidable dimagi Naxals in India were the sages who composed the Vedas and Upanishads – texts that the Hindutva brigade claims as the philosophical wellspring of their ideology.

Just last year, at an event in Ahmedabad, Home Minister Amit Shah shared his post-retirement plans: to study the Vedas and the Upanishads. While this interest in India’s ancient texts may appear commendable, a closer look at Vedic literature reveals a complex, pluralistic, and heterodox tradition that is fundamentally at odds with the ideology that Shah and his associates champion.

item.title: Prayer camps drive urban growth along Nigeria’s ‘spiritual highway’
item.description: The close proximity of Christian and Muslim camps has encouraged mutual borrowing of spatial forms and religious practices.
item.content:encoded:
The highway between Lagos and Ibadan was built in 1978 at the height of Nigeria’s oil boom. Lagos is the country’s largest city, with an estimated population of over 20 million, and Ibadan the third-largest and home to a globally renowned university.

But the boom years are over and rising traffic and decades of neglect have turned the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway into one of Nigeria’s deadliest motorways, earning it the nickname “highway of death”.

Yet even as the 127km stretch of road has faltered as a transport corridor linking north and south, it has flourished as a stage for public religion. Today, lined with sprawling prayer camps, it’s also known as the “spiritual highway”. Religious billboards have replaced road signs and religious camps have been established along the route.

For years my research as an anthropologist has explored how multi-faith settings challenge conventional ideas of religion. I have studied the more than 30 religious organisations that have established vast prayer camps along the course of the highway since the 1980s. Attracting tens of thousands of worshippers seeking health and wealth, they have transformed the expressway into an urban spiritual centre.

item.title: Karnataka minister B Nagendra resigns amid allegations of financial irregularities
item.description: The Congress leader accused the Bharatiya Janata Party of targeting him because he is a Dalit.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka minister B Nagendra resigned from the Cabinet on Friday amid pressure from the Opposition Bharatiya Janata Party over alleged financial irregularities in the Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribe Development Corporation, The Indian Express reported.

The alleged irregularities came to light in May 2024 after an accounts superintendent with the corporation died by suicide and left a note alleging unauthorised transfers of funds. The Congress leader was the tribal welfare minister at the time, but was not named in the case.

He stepped down in June 2024, saying that he wanted a fair investigation in the case. He was re-inducted into the Cabinet on August 3, a month after DK Shivakumar replaced Siddaramaiah as the chief minister.

On Friday, Nagendra accused the BJP of pressuring him to step down.

“I asked the BJP many times to discuss allegations against me in the Assembly but they did not come,” The Indian Express quoted him as saying. “Where is the proof?”

Nagendra alleged that he was being “attacked” because he is a Dalit.

item.title: SIR exercise: Citizenship test must be a balancing act
item.description: Beyond documentation, inclusive voting is based on the relationship between citizenship, evidence and democratic participation.
item.content:encoded:
A passport is the most recognisable document the Indian state issues to its citizens. It carries the national emblem, is issued by a sovereign government, and allows its holder to cross international borders as an Indian national.

Yet, during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, the Ministry of External Affairs clarified that an Indian passport should be understood primarily as a travel document rather than as conclusive proof of citizenship, a distinction that took on particular significance amid the SIR debate.

It is correctly established as a matter of law that a passport is not conclusive proof of citizenship. It is a travel document, issued under the Passports Act, 1967, a statute that itself permits passports to be issued to non-citizens in specified circumstances.

If a passport does not settle the question, what should an ordinary citizen produce when the state asks whether he/she may vote? The question reaches well beyond documentation. It goes to the relationship between citizenship, evidence and democratic participation.

The Election Commission has framed the SIR as an exercise meant to ensure that no eligible citizen is left off the rolls while no ineligible person is included on them. It undertook the exercise under Article 324 of the Constitution and Section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act,...

item.title: Bengal: 10 newborns dead in a day, 60 in three weeks at Malda medical college
item.description: The government has sought a report from the hospital on the matter and launched an inspection of nearby health facilities in the district.
item.content:encoded:
At least 60 newborns died in August till Monday at the West Bengal government-run Malda Medical College and Hospital, The Indian Express reported on Friday. Ten of these deaths were reported on Monday alone.

The state government has sought a report from the hospital on the infant deaths.

The authorities are also conducting inspections at other hospitals and nursing homes in the district, where many of the children were treated before being referred to the government facility, The Times of India reported.

Of the 10 newborns who died on Monday, eight were born at other hospitals or nursing homes in the district and were brought to the government medical college in critical condition, The Indian Express quoted hospital Superintendent Prosenjit Bar as saying.

Of the 60 deaths reported till Monday, 44 babies were born elsewhere and later referred to the hospital, the newspaper quoted unidentified state health department officials as saying.

The hospital officials said that while some infants suffered from respiratory distress, others had jaundice or heart problems, the newspaper reported.

On Wednesday, state Health Minister Shardwat Mukhopadhyay said that the infant mortality rate in Malda district has increased. “We have asked for a detailed report to understand why and how this happened,” The Indian Express quoted Mukhopadhyay as saying.

item.title: Is the Indian middle class dying?
item.description: The middle class is the government's cash cow but has lost political power, argues investor Saurabh Mukherjea.
item.content:encoded:
After independence, the middle class ruled India. High-quality university education, good urban infrastructure, and law and order in metros: the government strove to meet white collar India's needs.

Today, however, argues investor Saurabh Mukherjea, that is not the case. He says the middle class lacks political leverage despite contributing the most towards taxes.

In a new book, Breakpoint: The Crisis of the Middle Class and the Future of Work, Mukherjea, along with Nandita Rajhansa and Sapana Bhavsar, argues that falling employment, stagnant wages and exploding debt driven by social media envy means the Indian middle class is facing an existential crisis.

It was in the early nineties that India saw the emergence of compact disc (CD) systems, which revolutionised the audio business worldwide. Music was recorded onto the discs using lasers. Bush India had launched the country’s first CD player, assembled from components supplied by an undisclosed Japanese manufacturer. The CD system was sold for Rs 10,500. For good measure, Bush threw in a conventional cassette recorder and radio, too. After all, the market was still at a nascent stage.

Soon, Videocon, in collaboration with Toshiba, launched a CD player priced at seven thousand rupees. The only problem was they didn’t have the government’s clearance to manufacture CDs. In the absence of recording facilities, the music companies used Hong Kong as a base. Most people brought CDs whenever they travelled abroad. At the time, the number of CDs in the country was around 35,000. The 250% import duty on disc players was a major hassle. The manufacturers, though, expected a dramatic growth in the next five years.

item.title: India to buy Javelin anti-tank missiles from US, says envoy
item.description: The deal would open the door to co-production opportunities, United States Ambassador Sergio Gor said.
item.content:encoded:
India plans to buy Javelin anti-tank guided missile systems from the United States, US Ambassador Sergio Gor said on Friday.

In a post on social media, Gor said the purchase was a “great step forward” in the US-India defence relationship and opened the door to co-production opportunities. “The engagement between our two nations is at record high levels,” he wrote.

New Delhi is yet to comment on Gor’s announcement.

The Javelin is a portable anti-tank missile that can be carried and operated by a single soldier. It uses a “fire-and-forget” system, allowing the missile to track and hit its target without further guidance from the operator.

The weapons system is used by the US military, its partners in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and some other countries such as Ukraine and Saudi Arabia.

The potential Javelin deal comes amid deepening defence relations between the two countries.

In October, India and the US signed a 10-year framework for “major defence partnership”.

The US had designated India as its “major defence partner” in 2016. In 2018, India was elevated to tier one of the Strategic Trade Authorisation, which allows New Delhi to receive license-free access to a range of US military and dual-use technologies.

item.title: Lok Sabha strength should remain 543 for 25 years, Mallikarjun Kharge tells PM Modi
item.description: The Congress chief also sought an all-party meeting to discuss the Bharatiya Janata Party government’s proposed delimitation exercise.
item.content:encoded:

The process of fixing the boundaries of electoral constituencies is called delimitation.

Kharge also said that one-third reservation for women should be implemented from the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.

The Congress leader said that after the meeting on the government’s delimitation proposal, all political parties should be given adequate time to study it before it is introduced in any special session of Parliament the government may be considering.

He added that the delimitation proposal was a matter of “enormous significance” for the country and urged the government not to “bulldoze” it through again, as it had attempted to do on April 16 and 17.

During a three-day special session of Parliament in April, the Bharatiya Janata Party-led Union government introduced the 2026 Constitution 131st Amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha to amend the 2023 Women’s Reservation Act and redraw the boundaries of electoral constituencies.

item.title: Dried fig, bitter gourd, red onion: A new book brings chutney recipes with unique ingredients
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Chutney Chronicles: Recipes, Stories, Wellness’, by Sudha G Tilak.
item.content:encoded:
Chutney has travelled beyond the subcontinent in memory and migration. As trade routes, indenture and empire carried people and ingredients across oceans, chutneys travelled with them. In the Caribbean it became satini; in Southeast Asia, a cousin to sambal; in Britain, it evolved into sweet-sour flavours like Major Grey’s Chutney and Colonel Skinner’s Chutney and in South Africa, Mrs HS Ball’s Chutney remains a supermarket emblem of Indian migration. This chapter explores chutneys that embraced new landscapes and ingredients. Contemporary kitchens continue this dialogue by pairing matcha with coriander, romesco with red chilli, hummus with amla. These experiments remind us that chutney is migratory and gloriously hybrid. A condiment, yes. But also, a traveller.

Chocolate and anjeer chutney

You know those days when a mad idea seizes you? This chutney is the result of one of my ‘let-it-all-loose’ moments in the kitchen. It brings together luscious figs, dark chocolate and a splash of Cognac, with green chilli slipping in a sly kick. The result is a sweet– spicy preserve that pairs beautifully with cheese or warm sourdough. Inspired by both French and Indian culinary traditions, this chutney is a bold marriage of decadence and heat, an instant conversation starter on any table or cheeseboard.

It clarified that it was not asking for organisers to adopt an exclusively vegetarian approach, but suggested that “non-vegetarian” food stalls be kept in designated areas outside pandals.

“We are not unaware of Bengal’s culture or food habits,” Nirgunananda, a member of the VHP’s central advisory council, said. “Durga Puja in Bengal has never been synonymous with an exclusively vegetarian way of life.”

He claimed that the VHP’s concern was to keep the area around the deity “clean” and uphold the “sanctity and cleanliness” of the space immediately surrounding it.

“Non-vegetarian food can be sold at designated places, but its leftovers must not find their way into the pandal or contaminate the area around the deity,” he added.

item.title: Review: ‘Padatik’ is a half-done portrait of the iconic director Mrinal Sen
item.description: Srijit Mukherji’s Bengali film is out on Zee5.
item.content:encoded:
Bengali director Srijit Mukherji’s Padatik is named after one of the most well-regarded movies by his subject, the director Mrinal Sen. Mukherji’s Padatik (The Foot Soldier) suggests that the acclaimed filmmaker and his films were inseparable. Like the fictional character played by Dhritman Chatterjee in Sen’s 1973 classic, the Mrinal Sen conjured up by Mukherji is curious, combative, ideologically motivated and a fighter all the way through.

Mukherji’s Padatik was released in cinemas in 2024. Padatik is now being streamed on Zee5.

Filmed mostly in black and white by cinematographer Indranath Marick, Padatik is less of a biopic and more of a personal take on Sen’s lengthy life and career. Sen died in 2018 at the age of 95. His final film was Amar Bhuvan in 2002.

Mukherji’s Padatik reconstructs Sen’s life and career through key incidents. These include his early struggles to become a director, the near-destitution faced by him and his wife Geeta (Aishani Dey and Monami Ghosh), the intellectual ferment that produced Sen and to which he contributed equally.

In the global alt-right ecosystem, Kaliyuga – the spectre of the Hindu caste order turned upside down – has emerged as the central image representing the democratic world order. De-democratisation, says Alexandr Dugin, requires the overthrow of Kaliyuga, that is, in his words, “the present order of things, of which the core could be described as human rights, anti-hierarchy, and political correctness”. He had said this in Delhi in 2012, while attending a prestigious international social science conference, in an interview published by a magazine that declares its purpose “is to promote white identity politics”.

Kaliyuga – a Hindu term for an epoch of sexual and social degeneration caused by the collapse and corruption of caste hierarchy – has excellent traction in contemporary white-supremacist, alt-right and multipolarist discourse internationally, among ideologues, media figures and even political parties. item.description: Ambiecka Pandit’s Hindi film, written by Amita Vyas, is out on Prime Video.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: India’s first railway is disappearing bit by bit. Can we save what’s left?

The Great Indian Peninsula Railway – the GIPR – is the railway that operated India’s first commercial passenger line between Bombay and Thane in 1853. The Bombay-Thane line was not merely India’s first passenger railway route. It was the beginning of a system that transformed the country. The railway that began with three locomotives, 14 coaches and about 400 passengers on April 16, 1853. eventually grew into the vast Indian Railways network.

Today’s Central Railway suburban system in Mumbai still runs across much of that original landscape. That continuity is extraordinary. We should be proud of it. But pride cannot simply mean celebrating the first train every April 16 and then allowing the physical evidence of that story to disappear year after year.

This August, that question has arrived at Sion.

A portion of the old Sion railway station, on the original Bombay-Thane line of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, is being dismantled to make way for railway expansion. Among the elements that could disappear along with the old station hut (used as station manager’s cabin) are old iron roof brackets bearing the imprint of the GIPR era.

The sari represents a culture in which the woven and textured-with-pattern garment; unpierced or intruded upon by the stitching needle; was considered not only more appropriate in terms of aesthetics and climate, but was also an act of greater purity and simplicity. It is difficult to historically ascertain the sari’s evolution as a single piece drape, though in many parts of India (Kerala, the six northeast states, Rajasthan and Gujarat), its possible preceding versions of two or three-piece drapes, continue to be worn.

item.title: From Kerala to Kargil, ‘Muslim’ ecologies are syncretic and intertwined with the landscape
item.description: Hateful political rhetoric of land ‘jihad’ is ignorant of the deep and intimate history of Islam and the Indian landscape.
item.content:encoded:
In the vast mangrove delta of the Sundarbans, where the Bengal coast dissolves into tidal rivers and dense forest, survival depends on more than a boat and a net. Before entering the forest to collect honey or cut wood, fishermen and wood-gatherers stop at small shrines along the treeline to invoke Bonbibi, a figure one 19th traveller called a “strange goddess”, believed to be the keeper of the forest.

Bonbibi is, by origin, a Muslim figure. Her legend, interwoven with the tiger god Dakshin Ray and the mediating saint Ghazi Miyan, forms the cosmological grammar of an entire ecosystem: a shared sacred world in which tigers, humans, forest spirits, and Muslim saints negotiate the boundary between the wild and the habitable.

What, exactly, makes this a Muslim ecology? Not the presence of Muslims as such. Hindu, animist, and tribal communities too invoke Bonbibi. What makes it Muslim is that an Islamic idiom – a saint, a sacred genealogy, a moral vocabulary of protection and transgression drawn from Islamic devotional practice – has become one of the registers through which an entire regional community, across religious lines, understands and regulates its relationship with a dangerous and necessary landscape.

Scrolling through the tributes to Dolly Parton this morning – from the Grand Ole Opry, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, queerfluencers and others – I thought to myself: that’s her real name?

Yes. The “Queen of Country”, who died overnight aged 80, was born Dolly Rebecca Parton. My surprise at the authenticity of her name says something about the contradiction within the figure of Dolly.

A sometime figure of ridicule and satire, the opening image of Dolly – in interviews, send ups and even her own branding – was often related to her apparent “fakeness”.

Her literal figure – breasts, face, hair – was obviously artificial. And often these synthetic additions to her body were transposed into an assumption she herself was, if not inauthentic, at least somewhat superficial. Dolly’s first hit on the country charts was Dumb Blonde in 1967.

But what a name! Not a diminutive of a serious name, not a stage name, but a real name that moves us towards her celebrity image as one: dressed-up, made-up, an object with which the entertainment industry played.

In January 2025, Google announced one of the largest biochar carbon removal deals to date, agreeing to purchase 1,00,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide removal credits from Varaha ClimateAg Private Limited, a Gurugram-based climate tech startup. Biochar is a carbon-rich charcoal produced by heating organic matter in low-oxygen conditions, which can store carbon in soil for hundreds of years.

By January 2026, Varaha had added Microsoft to its roster of corporate buyers, with Lufthansa, Swiss Re, and Capgemini also signing offtake agreements.

Among Varaha’s initiatives is a project in Kachchh, Gujarat, combining carbon sequestration with ecosystem restoration.

item.title: Lessons from Egypt: How the autocratic President Hosni Mubarak struggled with stability and growth
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Shortest History of Egypt’, by Maria Golia.
item.content:encoded:
Hosni Mubarak was a rectangular man, built low to the ground, boxy and taurine. When Egyptians nicknamed him la vache qui rit (“the laughing cow”), after a popular brand of cheese spread, it was derisive yet reminiscent of old titles like “great bull”, evoking a king’s virility. In his suit, tie and Ray-Ban aviators, with his lovely wife and sons, Mubarak was the image of a modern family man, but no ordinary one. The day when former president Anwar El-Sadat and 11 others died, Mubarak was close enough to be spattered with their blood yet he survived virtually unscathed. As president, he took no chances in keeping with the adage “trust in Allah, but tie your camel first”, never lifting the state of emergency declared after Sadat’s assassination, granting his security apparatus carte blanche under martial law to act on his behalf. item.title: Why jobs are becoming unaffordable for some Indian women
item.description: Dalit or Muslim women often break barriers to secure formal employment, but struggle with the costs of living in a city while battling prejudice.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-three-year-old Ayesha* fought hard to study a master’s degree in social sciences and finally land a corporate job in Delhi in 2024. But within a year, she was struggling to stay afloat with her starting salary of Rs 40,000.

She was paying Rs 18,000 a month for a gated, paying guest accommodation, a metro-adjacent location and a neighbourhood she could come home to at night without planning ahead. After food, travel, groceries and sending money home, she was saving Rs 1,000 at best.

The latest annual Periodic Labour Force Survey data says that women’s workforce participation stood at 40% from January to December 2025. It means the number of Indian women working has nearly doubled from 23.3% in 2017-’18.

However, the rise in women’s workforce is largely among rural workers, and a significant part of it appears to be driven by a change in the definition that reclassified women performing subsistence and domestic tasks as “self-employed”.

These numbers also conceal the high costs paid by first-generation Dalit or Muslim women to attain a private sector job and remain employed in an Indian city. These are the women who are most likely to have broken through family resistance and constrained networks to land a job that offers upward mobility.

item.title: Why all eyes are on California’s billionaire wealth tax bill
item.description: The coming election will serve as an important test of the political power of the billionaire class, and the broader health of American democracy.
item.content:encoded:
In November, California will vote on a proposal to levy a one-off 5% tax on the wealth of all billionaires in the state.

Google co-founder and billionaire Sergey Brin has already spent US$100 million on political donations to a group opposing the tax. Brin is hoping to avoid a potential tax bill of US$13 billion, a return of roughly 130 to 1 if that investment is successful.

Advocates of the billionaire tax claim it would raise US$100 billion in revenue, to be allocated directly to state-funded healthcare, food assistance and public education.

Supporters of the union-backed proposal also highlight that most billionaires currently pay lower marginal rates of tax than the average worker, and that the revenue is desperately needed to fill gaps in funding created by US President Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid.

Its critics, which include California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, argue the measure will drive billionaires and their tax revenue to leave the state.

Taxing the ultrawealthy

Similar measures targeting the ultrawealthy are currently under consideration around the world.

It goes on well for a while. You gain access to and better understand a bewildering ecosystem of programmers, producers, sales agents and distributors. The pages of your passport fill up with visas from places you would never have been able to visit on your own dime.

The peepul of Sikandar Bagh! That is how the people of Lucknow know me. I am the tree that is the heart of the bagh, the centre around which it grew. My branches spread wide and many birds perch there. I cast a thick shade that travellers enjoy in the summer. And in winter, my Sikander Bagh comes alive with the sounds of laughter and of music. Crowds gather then to enjoy a musical evening, while the stars slowly flicker to life in the sky above.

item.title: Manipur: CRPF member shot, two homes burned in clashes between Kukis and Nagas
item.description: The violence took place along the bordering areas of the Kangpokpi and Senapati districts.
item.content:encoded:
A Central Reserve Police Force sub-inspector was shot and at least two homes were torched in Manipur after clashes broke out between two groups on Monday, The Hindu reported.

Sub-inspector Pradeep Singh of the 36th Battalion of the CRPF sustained a bullet injury to his left leg when he was caught in crossfire along the border of the Kuki-dominated Kangpokpi district and the Naga-dominated Senapati district, The Indian Express reported. He is being treated at the District Hospital, Senapati.

The violence began in the early hours of Monday when unknown miscreants burned down a home in the Taphou Kuki village in the Kangpokpi district. Soon afterwards, another home was torched in the Taphou Naga village in the Senapati district.

The two groups exchanged fire after 9 am, in which the CRPF member was injured, The Hindu reported.

Residents of Senapati district blocked the National Highway-2, also known as the Imphal-Dimapur (Nagaland) Road, for several hours. Transport services on the highway had resumed just last Friday, three years after the ethnic violence that broke out in the state in May 2023.

The Taphou Kuki village authority said it condemned the “highly deplorable, inhuman, and unacceptable” arson attack, and called for an end to violence, The Hindu reported.

item.title: Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh released from prison for 17th time since rape conviction
item.description: With this, the Dera Sacha Sauda chief has exhausted his annual entitlement of 10 weeks of parole and three weeks of furlough.
item.content:encoded:
Dera Sacha Sauda chief Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh walked out of jail on Tuesday after being granted a 21-day furlough, reported Hindustan Times. This is the 17th time he has been released from prison since he was convicted in a rape case in August 2017.

Singh is serving a 20-year prison sentence in Sunaria jail in Haryana’s Rohtak for raping two of his women disciples. During the furlough, he will stay at the headquarters of his organisation in Sirsa district.

This is his third consecutive temporary release during which he has been allowed to stay at the Sirsa headquarters, NDTV reported. At other times, he stayed at his organisation’s ashram in Uttar Pradesh’s Baghpat.

With the latest 21-day furlough, Singh has exhausted his annual entitlement of 10 weeks of parole and three weeks of furlough under the 2022 Haryana Good Conduct Prisoners Temporary Release Act.

The law allows prisoners a total of 10 weeks of parole in a calendar year, which can be taken in two parts, along with up to three weeks of furlough that must be availed in a single stretch.

item.title: A question of survival: Why Census 2027 must count Nomadic and Denotified Tribes separately
item.description: These communities live with the legacy of criminalisation but have never been recognised in national policies due to poor data about them.
item.content:encoded:
Census 2027 is crucial to the Nomadic and Denotified Tribes whose existence, culture, livelihood and identities are deeply connected to the fundamental right of being counted.

Community activists and leaders have repeatedly demanded that Nomadic and Denotified Tribes be counted separately in the Census. But these demands have been ignored even though the Census is much more than just counting people – it is fundamental to constitutional justice, policy-making and the equitable distribution of resources.

As someone from the Ghisadi Gadiya Lohar Nomadic and Denotified Tribe community, I have closely seen the effects of relentless migration, prejudice from settled populations, homelessness, the utter lack of safety and social security, little schooling and healthcare access and negligible democratic participation.

In almost all states, these communities are at the bottom of the caste hierarchy, below the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. There is no standard identity across the country: our caste identity keeps changing from state to state because there is no uniform counting of our people at the national level.

item.title: US moves to hike H-1B fee to over $100,000, revoke visas of asylum seekers

The United States on Monday proposed to impose a fee of over $100,000 on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers.

Additionally, the Donald Trump administration is also planning to revoke business and tourist visas of about 2,00,000 foreigners seeking asylum status in the United States, reported AP.

The US government had imposed a temporary H-1B visa registration fee in September. The order is slated to expire next month, when it completes one year. The regulation proposed by the US Department of Homeland Security, which was posted in the Federal Register on Monday, would make a $103,265 fee for H-1B permanent.

The fee, however, would not apply to foreigners already in the United States on student visas or to renewals of current visas.

H-1B non-immigrant visas allow US companies to temporarily employ highly skilled foreign workers in speciality occupations. Over the past few years, Indians have constituted the majority of H-1B visa holders. Indians comprised 71% of all H-1B visas issued by the US in the financial year 2023-’24.

item.title: How public canteens in India are creating jobs, supporting women, and fostering democratic spaces
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Freebies or Rights: Understanding Social Policy in India,’ by Reetika Khera.

Canteens are under-researched not only in India, but elsewhere too. Therefore, in November-December 2023, we conducted The Canteen Survey 2023 in three states – Karnataka, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. The purpose was to understand the role of canteens and how well or poorly they are implemented.

One persistent problem with canteen schemes is that they have fallen prey to petty politicking at the state level. This can take different forms: in Andhra Pradesh, Anna Canteens were closed en masse. In Karnataka, the Congress government introduced Indira Canteens in 2017. When the BJP government came to power in the state, there were budget cuts, layoffs and in some canteens, opening hours were curtailed. Tamil Nadu’s Amma Canteens, which started in 2013, benefited from the fact that the party that introduced the scheme (the AIADMK) remained in power until 2021. item.title: The desperate wait of families of Indian men tricked into fighting Russia’s war
item.description: Family members blamed a web of travel agents in India and Russia for entrapping their relatives.
item.content:encoded:
From the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine border, Manoj Singh Shekhawat sent a 21-second audio message to his family in Rajasthan on October 15.

“If you don’t hear from me for three days, consider that I am no more,” the 33-year-old cab driver from Jaipur told his family.

Ten months later, however, his family has not given up hope that he is alive.

“We hope that maybe they are making him work at some place where there is no internet connectivity,” said Ajay Singh Rathore, a cousin.

Shekhawat’s family is among 26 Indian families who moved the Supreme Court in March to direct the Union government to trace and repatriate their loved ones from the active conflict zone on the Russia-Ukraine border.

Since the outbreak of war between Russia and Ukraine in 2022, hundreds of Indians have found themselves fighting along the Russian Armed Forces. Many claimed to have been lured there by recruitment agents. It is illegal for Indian citizens to fight for another country.

Shekhawat was recruited by a local agent in Jaipur early last year on the promise of a high-paying job, his family said.

item.title: Living and longer and living well are not the same thing. Here’s why ‘healthspan’ matters more
item.description: The period of our lives we spend in good health is the goal we should be focusing on.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve spent more than three decades studying how exercise and diet keep us healthy. But one thing keeps showing up in the data: living longer and living well are not in sync. While we’ve partly solved the first one, we are lagging behind at the second.

Over the past century, the average Canadian’s life expectancy has increased by 22 years, to roughly 80 for men and 84 for women. Medical and scientific research may push those numbers higher. However, the number of years we can expect to live in good health has been declining, and in Canada it now stands at about 67, down from a peak of about 70 years.

That means a lot of us are on track to spend close to two decades, sometimes longer, living with chronic illness, cognitive decline or lost mobility. That gap, not lifespan itself, is the real crisis. And almost nobody treats it like one.

Longevity is the word on everyone’s lips, with influencers discussing the possibility of three-digit lifespans. item.title: Online ornamental plant trade could be pathway for invasive species into India
item.description: Retailers ship ship seeds, bulbs and live plants directly to people’s homes but there are feasible solutions to check this.
item.content:encoded:
One of the world’s top 100 worst invasive species was brought to India in the 19th century as an ornamental garden plant. But Lantana camara, which now occupies 40% of India’s tiger habitats, was not the only one.

The ornamental horticulture industry is recognised as a key global pathway for introducing invasive alien species. A new study examining India’s online ornamental plant trade has found that a majority of these plants sold online are alien species, many of which are known to be invasive or naturalised in other countries.

The study, published in Environmental Conservation, also revealed that 57 species already declared invasive in India were available for purchase online, including Lantana camara and the highly-invasive Parthenium hysterophorus.

Invasive alien species are recognised as one of five major drivers of global biodiversity decline. “They outcompete our native species and the cost is enormous,” said Kesang Bhutia, the study’s lead author and a graduate student at Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), Bengaluru.

“Not all alien plants are a threat. There is a continuum,” explained Bhutia. A newly-introduced plant cannot survive without human care. Some escape cultivation, enter native ecosystems and naturalise, reproducing independently. Others can go further to become invasive.
